evidence.label: Smooth isometric immersions of closed surfaces into Euclidean four-space

headline: Proves that every closed smooth curved surface can be placed in four-dimensional space with all its distances kept.
scope: Every closed smooth Riemannian surface, orientable or not, mapped smoothly into Euclidean four-space; self-intersections are allowed.
plain: A curved surface carries its own rule for measuring lengths, called a metric. An isometric immersion places the surface in flat space so that every length along it is kept, though the surface may pass through itself. Nash's general theorem needs 17 dimensions for surfaces, and Gromov reached five for closed ones. This paper proves that four dimensions always suffice for closed surfaces, and Lean checks the theorem.
doesNot: This does not give an embedding without self-intersections, and it does not cover three-dimensional space.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Mikhail Gromov, who explicitly recorded the question of smooth isometric immersion of surfaces into four-space
scorecard.significanceWhy: It lowers the known dimension for smooth isometric immersions of closed surfaces from five to four, with a Lean check.

explanation:
Take a flat torus, the surface you get by gluing opposite edges of a square without stretching. Give each side length 2π, about 6.283. The map that sends (x, y) to (cos x, sin x, cos y, sin y) places it in four-dimensional space. Moving in x traces a circle of radius 1 in the first two coordinates, at unit speed. Moving in y does the same in the last two. The two directions stay at right angles. So every length on the square is kept exactly. In ordinary three-dimensional space this is impossible for a flat closed surface. Any closed surface there has a point that curves like a sphere.

A closed surface is a finite surface with no edge, like a sphere or a torus. A Riemannian metric is a smooth rule for measuring lengths and angles on it. An isometric immersion is a smooth map into flat space that keeps every such length. Unlike an embedding, it may let the surface pass through itself[4]. The question is which dimension is always enough. Gromov recorded the four-dimensional question for surfaces[5]. He later traced it back to Chern around 1950. Nash's theorem works in dimension 17 for surfaces, since 2 × (3 × 2 + 11)/2 = 17[6]. Gromov later reached five dimensions for closed surfaces. Poznyak handled four dimensions, but only on flat planar regions[7].

The paper proves that four dimensions suffice[1]. Every closed smooth Riemannian surface has a smooth isometric immersion into four-space. No curvature limit is assumed, and surfaces with no consistent sides, like the Klein bottle, are included[2]. This lowers the known dimension for closed surfaces from five to four[3].

The proof has four stages[8]. It starts with a small map into a round three-dimensional sphere inside four-space, with lengths a bit too short. The missing length is split into finitely many simple pieces on small disks. Each piece is added by a fast circular wiggle in a direction at right angles to the surface. Small further corrections then make the lengths exact. The obstacle is keeping the bending of the surface usable for the next disk. The bending could vanish after one wiggle. The paper tracks it carefully through each step. Its exact correction needs no global inverse of the linearised equation[9].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of the main theorem. It covers every closed smooth Riemannian surface, with no orientability assumption. So the paper proves this, as far as the Lean statement matches the paper. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: A classical question settled for closed surfaces, with a Lean check. It allows self-intersections and says nothing about three-dimensional space. No specialist review is published.
